screens.title: Liskov Substitution & Interface Segregation
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will study two complementary SOLID principles that keep systems robust as they grow. First, the Liskov Substitution Principle asks that a subtype behave in every way an expected supertype can, so clients never encounter surprising behavior when objects are swapped. The classic square-versus-rectangle problem illustrates how a mathematically true relationship can still break software contracts. Second, the Interface Segregation Principle warns against large, catch-all interfaces that force classes to implement irrelevant operations. You will learn how to split fat interfaces into small, client-specific ones so implementations remain focused and tests remain small. Throughout we use concrete Python-style examples: a shape hierarchy, a photo-capable printer that must not break generic printing clients, and a multi-function device refactor into IPrinter, IScanner, and IFaxMachine. By the end you will recognize common LSP violations — such as strengthened preconditions, weakened postconditions, or unexpected exceptions — and you will know how to refactor fat interfaces into coherent capabilities. Think about a class you maintain now: does it promise behavior it cannot keep? That question will guide our practice.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to reason about correct subtype behavior and design focused interfaces that reduce unnecessary coupling. First, you will clearly define the Liskov Substitution Principle and identify when a subclass breaks a superclass’s behavioral contract. We will practice spotting violations such as unexpected exceptions, strengthened preconditions, or methods that change the expected semantics. Second, you will explain the Interface Segregation Principle and demonstrate how splitting a large interface into smaller role-specific interfaces reduces forced or dummy implementations. Third, you will apply both principles in practice: refactor a shape hierarchy to avoid substitution pitfalls, and refactor a multi-function device into IPrinter, IScanner, and IFaxMachine so clients depend only on needed capabilities. Finally, you will assess code examples and choose the safer design—composition, delegation, or interface splits—based on which preserves behavior and minimizes coupling. These objectives prepare you to refactor legacy code safely and to design new modules that remain flexible as requirements change.

screens.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
screens.narratorSegment: Liskov Substitution Principle is a behavioral rule: if S is a subtype of T, then code written to use T should operate correctly when given an S instead. That statement hides an important word — correctly — which means methods must preserve the expectations clients rely on: preconditions cannot be strengthened, postconditions cannot be weakened, and invariants must hold. In practice this means a subclass should not throw new exceptions or change return guarantees in ways that surprise existing callers. For example, a base type that promises a non-null return value must not have a subtype that sometimes returns null. A common design misconception is to assume matching method names is sufficient; matching behavior is the real requirement. A concrete example is a shape hierarchy: a Rectangle that allows independent width and height changes defines a contract. If a Square subtype enforces equal sides when either setter is called, client code that expects independent setters will observe different results. To keep systems safe designers can extract narrower interfaces or prefer composition over tight inheritance when behavioral contracts diverge. Takeaway: substitutability is about promises, not just signatures. Ask yourself: does the subtype keep the promise the base type made?

keyIdea.title: LSP in one line
keyIdea.text: Subtypes must honor the behavioral promises of their supertypes — contracts matter more than matching method names.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Liskov Substitution Principle
Definition and contract
LSP ties interfaces to behavior: preconditions, postconditions, and invariants define the contract.
Preconditions: Subclass must not require more to be true than the base type.
Postconditions: Subclass must fulfill at least the guarantees of the base type.
Invariants: Object state expectations must remain consistent across types.
Key Takeaway

LSP protects client code from surprising behavior by ensuring subtypes keep the promise made by supertypes.

Concrete example: contract check
Imagine a method that sets width to five and height to ten, then expects area fifty. If a subtype changes the setters to keep width and height equal, that expectation breaks. The problem is not that the class is mathematically related, but that its runtime behavior violates client expectations.
Common mistake
Assuming identical method names imply safe substitution. Behavioral guarantees are the true test.
Pro tip
If a subtype needs stronger checks or different guarantees, prefer a separate interface or composition, not an override that changes semantics.

screens.title: Square vs Rectangle — an LSP case study
screens.narratorSegment: The square-versus-rectangle example is a classic way to understand LSP in practice. Mathematically, every square is a rectangle, but software contracts change the story. Consider a Rectangle with independent setters for width and height. Clients expect to set these independently and to compute area accordingly. If Square inherits Rectangle and overrides setters to keep sides equal, a client that sets width and height separately will observe different area semantics. The essence of the violation is behavioral change: the Square enforces an invariant that the Rectangle did not promise. A concrete example: a test function sets width to five and height to ten and expects area fifty. With a Square instance substituting Rectangle, the area becomes one hundred, violating client expectations. A common misconception is to solve this by special-casing the client; that hides the deeper design problem. Better approaches include extracting a Shape interface for queries like area, or using composition so that Square and Rectangle share an internal shape representation without forcing one to be the other's subtype. Closing question: when you see shared mathematical relationships, do you inherit or compose?

keyIdea.title: Case study insight
keyIdea.text: Inheritance that matches math does not automatically preserve client behavior; prefer interfaces or composition when contracts differ.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Square vs Rectangle
What fails in practice
  • Clients expect independent setters; Square makes them coupled.
  • Tests that verify area after independent changes can fail when substituting Square.
  • The behavioral contract — not the type relation — is what matters.
Misconception
Just because a relationship is true mathematically doesn't mean it is safe as an inheritance relationship for all client code.
Design alternatives
Extract read-only Shape interface with area method; let Rectangle and Square implement it independently.
Use composition: Rectangle and Square contain a size object and expose behaviors without forcing subtype semantics.
Check your understanding

If a subclass must change a setter's semantics to preserve its invariant, inheritance is likely the wrong relationship.

screens.title: LSP violation: conceptual Python walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a small conceptual Python example that makes the LSP violation explicit. The code defines a Rectangle with set_width, set_height, and get_area methods. A Square subclass overrides both setters to enforce equal sides. A test function sets width to five and height to ten, then checks that area equals fifty. With a Rectangle the test passes. With a Square it fails because setting height also changes width. This failure demonstrates that the Square changed the behavioral contract the Rectangle implied. The lesson is not syntax but semantics: the subclass altered postconditions observable by clients. A common corrective action is to avoid making Square a subtype of Rectangle. Instead, define a Shape interface with an area method, or implement Square and Rectangle separately and share code through composition. When reading similar code, ask: does the subclass change what callers can rely on? If the answer is yes, refactor. In summary, tests that assert observable behavior are the best detectors of violation; use them to protect contracts while you refactor. LSP violation: conceptual Python walkthrough means behavioral tests that check client expectations reveal lsp violations quickly; prefer refactor over special-casing.. In practical terms, inspect the test that reveals the broken contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test-driven detection
keyIdea.text: Behavioral tests that check client expectations reveal LSP violations quickly; prefer refactor over special-casing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Python Walkthrough 
class Rectangle:
    def __init__(self, width, height):
        self._width = width
        self._height = height

    def set_width(self, width):
        self._width = width

    def set_height(self, height):
        self._height = height

    def get_area(self):
        return self._width * self._height

class Square(Rectangle):
    def __init__(self, side):
        super().__init__(side, side)

    def set_width(self, width):
        self._width = width
        self._height = width

    def set_height(self, height):
        self._width = height
        self._height = height

def test_area(rectangle):
    rectangle.set_width(5)
    rectangle.set_height(10)
    print('Expected 50, got', rectangle.get_area())
Narrative walkthrough
The test sets two independent properties and asserts a calculation. A subclass that couples those setters violates the implicit assumptions of that test. Tests that express observable client behavior are therefore the right place to detect substitution problems and drive refactoring decisions.
Pro tip: Keep behavioral tests small and specific; they act as contracts when you refactor types.

screens.title: Behavioral Contract — preconditions and postconditions
screens.narratorSegment: Behavioral contracts are the precise promises a type makes to its clients: what it expects to be true before a call and what it guarantees afterward. Preconditions are the caller's responsibilities; subclasses may not require more. Postconditions are the callee's guarantees; subclasses must provide at least as much. Invariants are internal truths that must remain valid across visible operations. Thinking in these terms helps you detect LSP violations: if a subclass strengthens a precondition, it demands more from callers and breaks substitutability. If it weakens a postcondition, it fails to deliver the promised results. For instance, if a base method guarantees a non-null return, a subtype that sometimes returns null is weakening that postcondition and violating LSP. A common misconception is that only runtime exceptions matter; silent weakening of results is equally harmful because client logic can silently make wrong decisions. To practice, write small specs for public methods and assert them in tests. Design choices that preserve preconditions, maintain postconditions, and keep invariants intact will keep your inheritance safe. Behavioral Contract — preconditions and postconditions means document preconditions, postconditions, and invariants for public methods; use them as refactoring safeguards.. In practical terms, how to reason about what a class promises. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Document preconditions, postconditions, and invariants for public methods; use them as refactoring safeguards.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Behavioral Contract
Preconditions, postconditions, invariants
  • Precondition: what the caller must ensure before calling.
  • Postcondition: what the method guarantees after it returns.
  • Invariant: state that must always hold for the object.
Example
If a method promises non-null results, a subtype returning null weakens the postcondition and breaks substitutability.
Practice prompt
For a public method in a class you maintain, write a one-line precondition and postcondition. Use tests to assert them. When refactoring a subtype, run those tests first to detect contract changes early.

screens.title: Common LSP violations and pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring patterns that lead to LSP violations. First, subclasses that throw exceptions the base method never threw. If client code never expects an exception, suddenly seeing one breaks control flow and can crash systems. Second, strengthened preconditions: if a subclass requires more from callers than the base class did, code that used to work will now fail. Third, weakened postconditions: a subtype that returns less precise results or null when the base guarantees a value will silently break logic. Another pitfall is altering method side effects — changing state in ways clients don't anticipate. A practical example: a base logger returns success True after writing; a subclass that returns None changes the observable contract. When you see these patterns, refactor the hierarchy: extract interfaces, use composition, or create a new subtype that does not inherit the original contract. Tests that codify expected behavior are the most reliable defense. Always question whether a subclass truly shares the same observable promises as the base type before you use inheritance. Common LSP violations and pitfalls means look for new exceptions, stronger requirements, weakened guarantees, or unexpected side effects as signs of broken substitutability.. In practical terms, exceptions, changed semantics, and return guarantees. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Common Violations
Watch for these pitfalls
  • Unexpected exceptions raised by subclass methods.
  • Strengthening preconditions so callers must do more work.
  • Weakening postconditions or returning null where a value was promised.
  • Changing side effects that clients rely upon.
Common mistake: treating inheritance as code reuse without checking the contract; reuse should not change observable behavior.
Defensive action
Write small behavioral tests for public methods and run them when refactoring. If tests fail, prefer composition or a new separate type rather than forcing the subtype to match an incompatible contract.

screens.title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
screens.narratorSegment: The Interface Segregation Principle says: clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. In practice this means prefer many small, cohesive interfaces over one large 'fat' interface. A fat interface forces implementers to provide irrelevant methods, leading to empty, dummy, or unsupported implementations that are code smells. For example, an IWorker with work, eat, sleep, and manage_team may be reasonable for a human worker but forces a robot worker to implement irrelevant behaviors. ISP encourages splitting such an interface into focused roles like IWorkable, IEatable, ISleepable, and IManageable. Clients that only need printing should depend only on IPrinter, not a multi-function device interface that includes scanning and faxing. A common misconception is to split interfaces into overly tiny bits that lack cohesion; balance matters. The goal is to make each interface represent a meaningful role so that implementers only depend on methods they actually need. Ask when an interface forces dummy implementations, then consider whether it should be split. Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) means design interfaces so that clients depend only on the behaviors they actually need, avoiding forced or dummy implementations.. In practical terms, designing narrow interfaces for client-specific needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ISP in one line
keyIdea.text: Design interfaces so that clients depend only on the behaviors they actually need, avoiding forced or dummy implementations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Interface Segregation
Why small interfaces help
Smaller interfaces keep implementing classes focused and reduce the need for empty or dummy method bodies. They also minimize the ripple effect when interfaces change.
Benefit: Implementers only implement what they use, simplifying tests and reducing coupling.
Benefit: Clients depend on narrow contracts and are insulated from unrelated changes.
Example: Worker interface
A RobotWorker forced to implement eat or sleep methods shows a fat interface smell. Splitting interfaces into roles keeps RobotWorker minimal and clear.
Key takeaway: Split only when methods form cohesive roles; avoid fragmentation that sacrifices clarity.

screens.title: ISP example: fat interface to role-specific interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine a concrete ISP example. A fat IWorker interface lists work, eat, sleep, and manage_team. HumanWorker might implement all methods, but RobotWorker is forced to provide empty bodies for irrelevant methods. This smells like unnecessary coupling and test overhead. The refactor is straightforward: decompose IWorker into IWorkable, IEatable, ISleepable, and IManageable. Then implement HumanWorker as a composition of those roles and RobotWorker as only IWorkable. A client that only needs work now depends on IWorkable and cannot accidentally call eat on a robot. The practical benefit is that changes to IEatable do not affect classes that only implement IWorkable. A common pitfall is over-splitting—create interfaces that represent meaningful capabilities rather than single trivial methods. When you refactor, also update clients to depend on the narrow interfaces, not the original fat interface. This reduces the coupling surface and keeps your implementation classes minimal and purposeful. In practical terms, transforming iworker into focused interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Design checklist: When to inherit, when to compose, when to split
screens.narratorSegment: When facing a design decision about inheritance or interfaces, apply a short checklist. First, ask whether the subtype truly preserves the observable behavior clients expect — if no, do not inherit. Second, ask whether methods on an interface represent cohesive behavior for a role; if not, split the interface into smaller capabilities. Third, if a subtype needs to alter core behavior for its own invariant, prefer composition or delegation to inheritance. Fourth, write or run behavioral tests that encode client expectations before refactoring; tests guide safe changes. Fifth, avoid creating dozens of single-method interfaces without cohesion; each interface should represent a meaningful capability used by clients. For a concrete example, when a PhotoPrinter needs extra photo-specific behavior, add a print_photo method instead of breaking generic printing. When a device only prints, make it depend on IPrinter, not a multi-function interface. This decision flow reduces surprises, narrows test scope, and keeps modules easier to reason about and maintain. screens.title: Assessment & troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Now apply what you've learned to identify violations and propose fixes. Question one: a Bird base class has a fly method. Penguin inherits Bird but cannot fly and raises an unsupported operation if fly is called. This violates LSP because Penguin cannot fulfill the base promise; better designs include introducing an IFlyable role that only flying birds implement, or making Bird more general so flight is optional and expressed through a separate capability. Question two: a DataProcessor interface requires read, transform, and write. A DataReader class only needs read but is forced to supply dummy transform and write methods. This breaks the Interface Segregation Principle. The remedy is to split the processor into IDataReader, IDataTransformer, and IDataWriter so each client depends only on the methods it uses. When troubleshooting real code, look for dummy implementations, unexpected exceptions from subtypes, and tests that fail after substitution. Each failing test points to a broken contract; fix by refactoring to composition or interface splits, and then update tests to represent the preserved promises. The core skill is to translate failing behavior into a minimal, safe design change.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will study two complementary SOLID principles that keep systems robust as they grow. First, the Liskov Substitution Principle asks that a subtype behave in every way an expected supertype can, so clients never encounter surprising behavior when objects are swapped. The classic square-versus-rectangle problem illustrates how a mathematically true relationship can still break software contracts. Second, the Interface Segregation Principle warns against large, catch-all interfaces that force classes to implement irrelevant operations. You will learn how to split fat interfaces into small, client-specific ones so implementations remain focused and tests remain small. Throughout we use concrete Python-style examples: a shape hierarchy, a photo-capable printer that must not break generic printing clients, and a multi-function device refactor into IPrinter, IScanner, and IFaxMachine. By the end you will recognize common LSP violations — such as strengthened preconditions, weakened postconditions, or unexpected exceptions — and you will know how to refactor fat interfaces into coherent capabilities. Think about a class you maintain now: does it promise behavior it cannot keep? That question will guide our practice.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to reason about correct subtype behavior and design focused interfaces that reduce unnecessary coupling. First, you will clearly define the Liskov Substitution Principle and identify when a subclass breaks a superclass’s behavioral contract. We will practice spotting violations such as unexpected exceptions, strengthened preconditions, or methods that change the expected semantics. Second, you will explain the Interface Segregation Principle and demonstrate how splitting a large interface into smaller role-specific interfaces reduces forced or dummy implementations. Third, you will apply both principles in practice: refactor a shape hierarchy to avoid substitution pitfalls, and refactor a multi-function device into IPrinter, IScanner, and IFaxMachine so clients depend only on needed capabilities. Finally, you will assess code examples and choose the safer design—composition, delegation, or interface splits—based on which preserves behavior and minimizes coupling. These objectives prepare you to refactor legacy code safely and to design new modules that remain flexible as requirements change.

This second objectives page focuses on how you'll practice and be assessed. You will run a hands-on activity: design a multi-functional printer system that demonstrates both LSP-safe behavior and ISP adherence. You will implement a Printer base, a BasicPrinter, and a PhotoPrinter that preserves generic printing behavior while adding photo-specific capabilities. Next, you will create IPrinter, IScanner, and IFaxMachine interfaces and show how a SimplePrinter depends only on IPrinter while an AdvancedMultiFunctionDevice composes all three. You will also answer conceptual assessment questions: for a Bird and Penguin example, identify why raising an unsupported operation violates substitutability and suggest refactors. Finally, you'll defend design choices: when to prefer interface splitting over composition, and how to avoid creating too many tiny interfaces that lack cohesion. These practices will prepare you to detect violations in legacy code and to design future modules that scale without surprising their clients.

Liskov Substitution Principle is a behavioral rule: if S is a subtype of T, then code written to use T should operate correctly when given an S instead. That statement hides an important word — correctly — which means methods must preserve the expectations clients rely on: preconditions cannot be strengthened, postconditions cannot be weakened, and invariants must hold. In practice this means a subclass should not throw new exceptions or change return guarantees in ways that surprise existing callers. For example, a base type that promises a non-null return value must not have a subtype that sometimes returns null. A common design misconception is to assume matching method names is sufficient; matching behavior is the real requirement. A concrete example is a shape hierarchy: a Rectangle that allows independent width and height changes defines a contract. If a Square subtype enforces equal sides when either setter is called, client code that expects independent setters will observe different results. To keep systems safe designers can extract narrower interfaces or prefer composition over tight inheritance when behavioral contracts diverge. Takeaway: substitutability is about promises, not just signatures. Ask yourself: does the subtype keep the promise the base type made?

The square-versus-rectangle example is a classic way to understand LSP in practice. Mathematically, every square is a rectangle, but software contracts change the story. Consider a Rectangle with independent setters for width and height. Clients expect to set these independently and to compute area accordingly. If Square inherits Rectangle and overrides setters to keep sides equal, a client that sets width and height separately will observe different area semantics. The essence of the violation is behavioral change: the Square enforces an invariant that the Rectangle did not promise. A concrete example: a test function sets width to five and height to ten and expects area fifty. With a Square instance substituting Rectangle, the area becomes one hundred, violating client expectations. A common misconception is to solve this by special-casing the client; that hides the deeper design problem. Better approaches include extracting a Shape interface for queries like area, or using composition so that Square and Rectangle share an internal shape representation without forcing one to be the other's subtype. Closing question: when you see shared mathematical relationships, do you inherit or compose?

Let's walk through a small conceptual Python example that makes the LSP violation explicit. The code defines a Rectangle with set_width, set_height, and get_area methods. A Square subclass overrides both setters to enforce equal sides. A test function sets width to five and height to ten, then checks that area equals fifty. With a Rectangle the test passes. With a Square it fails because setting height also changes width. This failure demonstrates that the Square changed the behavioral contract the Rectangle implied. The lesson is not syntax but semantics: the subclass altered postconditions observable by clients. A common corrective action is to avoid making Square a subtype of Rectangle. Instead, define a Shape interface with an area method, or implement Square and Rectangle separately and share code through composition. When reading similar code, ask: does the subclass change what callers can rely on? If the answer is yes, refactor. In summary, tests that assert observable behavior are the best detectors of violation; use them to protect contracts while you refactor. LSP violation: conceptual Python walkthrough means behavioral tests that check client expectations reveal lsp violations quickly; prefer refactor over special-casing.. In practical terms, inspect the test that reveals the broken contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Behavioral contracts are the precise promises a type makes to its clients: what it expects to be true before a call and what it guarantees afterward. Preconditions are the caller's responsibilities; subclasses may not require more. Postconditions are the callee's guarantees; subclasses must provide at least as much. Invariants are internal truths that must remain valid across visible operations. Thinking in these terms helps you detect LSP violations: if a subclass strengthens a precondition, it demands more from callers and breaks substitutability. If it weakens a postcondition, it fails to deliver the promised results. For instance, if a base method guarantees a non-null return, a subtype that sometimes returns null is weakening that postcondition and violating LSP. A common misconception is that only runtime exceptions matter; silent weakening of results is equally harmful because client logic can silently make wrong decisions. To practice, write small specs for public methods and assert them in tests. Design choices that preserve preconditions, maintain postconditions, and keep invariants intact will keep your inheritance safe. Behavioral Contract — preconditions and postconditions means document preconditions, postconditions, and invariants for public methods; use them as refactoring safeguards.. In practical terms, how to reason about what a class promises. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

There are a few recurring patterns that lead to LSP violations. First, subclasses that throw exceptions the base method never threw. If client code never expects an exception, suddenly seeing one breaks control flow and can crash systems. Second, strengthened preconditions: if a subclass requires more from callers than the base class did, code that used to work will now fail. Third, weakened postconditions: a subtype that returns less precise results or null when the base guarantees a value will silently break logic. Another pitfall is altering method side effects — changing state in ways clients don't anticipate. A practical example: a base logger returns success True after writing; a subclass that returns None changes the observable contract. When you see these patterns, refactor the hierarchy: extract interfaces, use composition, or create a new subtype that does not inherit the original contract. Tests that codify expected behavior are the most reliable defense. Always question whether a subclass truly shares the same observable promises as the base type before you use inheritance. Common LSP violations and pitfalls means look for new exceptions, stronger requirements, weakened guarantees, or unexpected side effects as signs of broken substitutability.. In practical terms, exceptions, changed semantics, and return guarantees. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Interface Segregation Principle says: clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. In practice this means prefer many small, cohesive interfaces over one large 'fat' interface. A fat interface forces implementers to provide irrelevant methods, leading to empty, dummy, or unsupported implementations that are code smells. For example, an IWorker with work, eat, sleep, and manage_team may be reasonable for a human worker but forces a robot worker to implement irrelevant behaviors. ISP encourages splitting such an interface into focused roles like IWorkable, IEatable, ISleepable, and IManageable. Clients that only need printing should depend only on IPrinter, not a multi-function device interface that includes scanning and faxing. A common misconception is to split interfaces into overly tiny bits that lack cohesion; balance matters. The goal is to make each interface represent a meaningful role so that implementers only depend on methods they actually need. Ask when an interface forces dummy implementations, then consider whether it should be split. Let's examine a concrete ISP example. A fat IWorker interface lists work, eat, sleep, and manage_team. HumanWorker might implement all methods, but RobotWorker is forced to provide empty bodies for irrelevant methods. This smells like unnecessary coupling and test overhead. The refactor is straightforward: decompose IWorker into IWorkable, IEatable, ISleepable, and IManageable. Then implement HumanWorker as a composition of those roles and RobotWorker as only IWorkable. A client that only needs work now depends on IWorkable and cannot accidentally call eat on a robot. The practical benefit is that changes to IEatable do not affect classes that only implement IWorkable. A common pitfall is over-splitting—create interfaces that represent meaningful capabilities rather than single trivial methods. When you refactor, also update clients to depend on the narrow interfaces, not the original fat interface. This reduces the coupling surface and keeps your implementation classes minimal and purposeful. This exercise asks you to implement a Printer base and a PhotoPrinter subclass that does not violate LSP. The principle is simple: any client that uses Printer. print_document must be able to use PhotoPrinter safely. A dangerous approach is for PhotoPrinter to override print_document to accept only photo formats or to raise errors for generic documents. Instead, implement print_document on PhotoPrinter to handle generic documents — perhaps by converting them to printable images — and expose a separate print_photo method for photo-specific paths. The chapter's starter code demonstrates this pattern by showing how PhotoPrinter provides print_document while offering print_photo as an additional capability. In the multi-function device scenario, a single IMultiFunctionDevice interface with print, scan, and fax methods creates unnecessary obligations for implementers that do not support all capabilities. The refactor decomposes this fat interface into three cohesive interfaces: IPrinter, IScanner, and IFaxMachine. A SimplePrinter implements only IPrinter; an AdvancedMultiFunctionDevice implements all three. Clients that require only printing depend on IPrinter and remain insulated from changes to scanning or fax functionality. This decomposition reduces test surface and prevents classes from carrying irrelevant methods. When refactoring, update clients to depend on the narrow interfaces and consider using composition in the AdvancedMultiFunctionDevice: delegate print to a printing component, scan to a scanner component, and fax to a fax component. That keeps each capability replaceable and testable. Beware over-fragmentation: each interface should represent a coherent behavioral role, not a single trivial method without context. The design tradeoff here improves modularity and limits the ripple of changes in large codebases. When facing a design decision about inheritance or interfaces, apply a short checklist. First, ask whether the subtype truly preserves the observable behavior clients expect — if no, do not inherit. Second, ask whether methods on an interface represent cohesive behavior for a role; if not, split the interface into smaller capabilities. Third, if a subtype needs to alter core behavior for its own invariant, prefer composition or delegation to inheritance. Fourth, write or run behavioral tests that encode client expectations before refactoring; tests guide safe changes. Fifth, avoid creating dozens of single-method interfaces without cohesion; each interface should represent a meaningful capability used by clients. For a concrete example, when a PhotoPrinter needs extra photo-specific behavior, add a print_photo method instead of breaking generic printing. When a device only prints, make it depend on IPrinter, not a multi-function interface. This decision flow reduces surprises, narrows test scope, and keeps modules easier to reason about and maintain. Now apply what you've learned to identify violations and propose fixes. Question one: a Bird base class has a fly method. Penguin inherits Bird but cannot fly and raises an unsupported operation if fly is called. This violates LSP because Penguin cannot fulfill the base promise; better designs include introducing an IFlyable role that only flying birds implement, or making Bird more general so flight is optional and expressed through a separate capability. Question two: a DataProcessor interface requires read, transform, and write. A DataReader class only needs read but is forced to supply dummy transform and write methods. This breaks the Interface Segregation Principle. The remedy is to split the processor into IDataReader, IDataTransformer, and IDataWriter so each client depends only on the methods it uses. When troubleshooting real code, look for dummy implementations, unexpected exceptions from subtypes, and tests that fail after substitution. Each failing test points to a broken contract; fix by refactoring to composition or interface splits, and then update tests to represent the preserved promises. The core skill is to translate failing behavior into a minimal, safe design change.

Let's review the essential ideas. First, the Liskov Substitution Principle: subtypes must be substitutable for their supertypes without changing program correctness. This centers on preserving behavioral contracts — preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. Second, behavioral contracts are practical tools: write small tests that encode what clients expect and use them to detect violations. Third, the Interface Segregation Principle: prefer narrow, cohesive interfaces over fat ones so implementers aren’t forced into dummy methods. Finally, the practical rule: when behavior diverges, prefer composition or a new interface rather than changing superclass semantics. These concepts help you design systems that remain maintainable, reduce test surface, and avoid surprising client code. Keep asking whether a type keeps the promises it makes and whether clients only depend on the behavior they need.
